late-113.title: Rising seas flood the Persian Gulf
late-113.text: For most of the ice age, the Persian Gulf was a dry basin. About 15,000 years ago, seas swollen by melting ice sheets began to flood it. The filling was slow. Much of the Gulf floor was still dry 12,000 to 9,000 years ago. The modern marine Gulf took shape in the early Holocene, by about 6,000 years ago.

late-112.title: The Missoula floods scour the Scablands
late-112.text: An ice dam on the Clark Fork River held back Glacial Lake Missoula, up to about 2,500 km³ of water. The dam kept failing and re-forming. Between 15,000 and 13,000 years ago it unleashed dozens of floods, about one every 55 years. The largest discharged about 10 km³ an hour. It swept across eastern Washington and into Oregon's Willamette Valley. Together the floods stripped about 210 km³ of loess, sediment and basalt from the land, carving the Channeled Scablands.

late-111.title: The Altai megaflood
late-111.text: Near the end of the last glaciation, glaciers in the Altai Mountains dammed the Chuya River. A large lake, holding up to 600 km³, filled the Chuya and Kurai basins. According to some geomorphologists, it burst in cataclysmic floods down the Katun River. The floods left giant ripples in the ground, up to 18 m high.

late-115.title: Magdalenian hunters return to the north
late-115.text: The Magdalenian reindeer hunters, 21,000 to 13,000 years ago, descended mainly from Gravettian groups who had sheltered in southwestern Europe during the Last Glacial Maximum. Around 15,000 years ago, after the harsh Oldest Dryas, they moved north again. They reached Britain and, eastward, Poland. From about 14,000 years ago, Western Hunter-Gatherers linked to the Epigravettian spread north across the Alps and largely replaced them.

late-114.title: The cave lion dies out
late-114.text: Cave lions vanished almost at once across their whole range, about 15,000 to 14,000 years ago. In North America they hung on roughly 1,000 years longer. They were already weakened. A population bottleneck between 47,000 and 18,000 years ago, probably driven partly by unstable climate, had cut their genetic diversity. The final cause is unknown. Climate change, shrinking prey and competition with other carnivores and humans have all been suggested.

late-116.title: The Antarctic Cold Reversal
late-116.text: While the north warmed, the far south turned cold. Between 14,700 and 13,000 years ago, the Southern Hemisphere south of 40° S saw intense cooling of air and ocean. Temperatures fell, carbon dioxide stopped rising and glaciers advanced again, as in New Zealand's Southern Alps. Tasmania records a matching cold spell. A meltwater pulse, probably from the Antarctic or Laurentide ice sheet, is thought to have caused it. It may have pushed the southern polar front north and brought more rain and snow to the Andes. After about 13,000 years ago warming resumed, and glaciers pulled back abruptly from the moraines they had built.

late-117.title: The Bølling–Allerød warming
late-117.text: About 14,690 years ago, the Northern Hemisphere warmed abruptly. This was the start of the Bølling–Allerød interstadial, a warm interval that lasted until about 12,890 years ago. Greenland's NorthGRIP ice core records the onset at 14,600 years ago, and methane in the air rose about 14,700 years ago. The engine was the ocean. A stronger Atlantic overturning circulation carried heat north. Meanwhile the Southern Hemisphere cooled, as told in {{ref:late-116}}. This tug-of-war, with one hemisphere warming as the other cools, is called the 'polar seesaw'. By the Allerød phase, temperatures in the northern Atlantic had climbed almost to present-day levels. The warmth reopened the north. People spread back across Eurasia from the refuges where they had sheltered during the glacial peak. In Beringia, shrub tundra replaced dry steppe after 14,000 years ago.

late-118.title: Meltwater pulse 1A: the fastest sea-level rise
late-118.text: In about 400 to 500 years, global sea level rose 16 to 25 m. That is roughly 40 to 60 mm a year, the fastest known rate of rise since the ice age. This surge, meltwater pulse 1A, is blamed on the rapid collapse of continental ice sheets. It began with, or just after, the abrupt Bølling–Allerød warming recorded in Greenland ice. The West Antarctic ice sheet shrank between 15,000 and 14,000 years ago, matching an abrupt rise around 14,500 years ago. Of all the named meltwater pulses, it is the most widely recognized and least disputed.

late-119.title: The African humid period begins
late-119.text: Lake Victoria was dry around 15,000 years ago. Then North Africa turned wetter, about 14,600 to 14,500 years ago, as Heinrich event 1 ended and the Bølling–Allerød warming began. Summer sunshine at least 4% stronger than today's, aided by changes in plants, dust and greenhouse gases, strengthened the African monsoon. Lake Victoria refilled and overflowed. Lakes Albert and Tana spilled into the White and Blue Nile, and the Nile took its current form about 15,000 years ago. Lakes such as Lake Chad formed or grew, glaciers grew on Kilimanjaro, and the Sahara shrank.

late-120.title: Monte Verde, a camp at the end of the Americas
late-120.text: In southern Chile, about 14,500 years ago, people built a tent-like structure about 20 feet long from wood and animal hides. This settlement, Monte Verde II, is one of the widely accepted sites older than Clovis. Its people were probably territorial, living in their river basin most of the year alongside late Pleistocene megafauna.

late-121.title: The Natufians settle down before farming
late-121.text: People in the Levant settled into villages before they farmed. The Natufian culture, radiocarbon-dated to 12,500 to 9,500 BC, supported sedentary or semi-sedentary communities. Its settlements were larger and more permanent than earlier ones. Some had round stone buildings, as at Ain Mallaha, and they hold the first evidence of food storage. Natufians harvested wild cereals and hunted gazelles. Then the cold, dry Younger Dryas pushed early settled groups back toward a more mobile life.

late-122.title: Paisley Caves and the oldest DNA in North America
late-122.text: Fossilized human dung from Oregon's Paisley Caves, radiocarbon dated to about 14,300 to 14,400 years ago, holds the oldest human DNA found in North America. The DNA ties these pre-Clovis people to Siberia or Asia. They ate plants, seeds, rodents, fish and insects. Critics question whether the coprolites are human and whether their dates hold. They suspect that human DNA leached into them later.

late-123.title: The Great Lakes basins begin to fill
late-123.text: The Great Lakes sit in holes the ice dug. Around 14,000 years ago, retreating ice sheets exposed the basins they had carved, and meltwater filled them. In Wisconsin, too, the ice began to retreat about then as the climate warmed.

late-124.title: The Older Dryas cold snap
late-124.text: Between the warm Bølling and Allerød phases, about 14,000 years ago, came a brief cold stadial, the Older Dryas. Its dates vary by about 400 years between methods, but it lasted only a century or two. Ice advanced again in places, as in the Littleton–Bethlehem readvance and Canada's Shulie Lake phase.

late-127.title: The Americas lose their megafauna
late-127.text: Every mammal over 1,000 kg in the Americas disappeared. About 72% of North American and 83% of South American megafaunal species died out. In North America the losses clustered around 13,800 to 11,400 years ago, with the onset of the Younger Dryas and the Clovis culture. Across the Americas they spanned 3,000 years at most. Ground sloths, litopterns and the last notoungulates vanished from the mainland around 12,000 years ago, along with most other large mammals. People did hunt them. Butchered bones, such as an Ohio ground sloth dated 13,738 to 13,435 years ago, prove it. Whether hunting, climate change or both caused the extinctions is a long-running controversy, though most scholars accept at least some human role. The loss even touched the air. Without the American megafauna, methane production is estimated to have fallen by about 9.6 million tons a year.

late-128.title: An ice-free corridor opens east of the Rockies
late-128.text: By 21,000 years ago, the Cordilleran and Laurentide ice sheets had merged east of the Rocky Mountains, closing the way into North America's interior. A gap between them opened about 13,800 ± 500 years ago, by 2022 estimates. Older studies put it at 13,000 to 12,000 years ago. Either way, that is later than the earliest widely accepted archaeological sites. The corridor could not have carried the first people south.

late-129.title: The Clovis culture spreads across North America
late-129.text: At Blackwater Draw in New Mexico, stone tools lay among the bones of Columbian mammoths. This is the type site of the Clovis culture, which spanned about 13,050 to 12,750 years ago. Its hallmark was the fluted Clovis point, a large leaf-shaped spear point also used for cutting. Clovis people were mobile hunter-gatherers who relied on big game, especially mammoths. They may have contributed to the megafauna extinctions, a controversial idea. They were not the first Americans. A 2022 study found the ice-free corridor impassable until about 13,800 years ago, long after people had reached lands south of the ice. From about 12,750 to 12,600 years ago, Clovis gave way to regional cultures such as Folsom.

late-130.title: The Laacher See eruption
late-130.text: About 13,006 years ago, a VEI 6 eruption in western Germany, comparable to Pinatubo in 1991, expelled about 6 km³ of magma. It left the crater lake of Laacher See. Its ash dammed the Rhine into a lake of 140 km². When that dam broke, the outburst flood left deposits as far as Bonn. Research in the 1990s proposed it as the trigger of the Younger Dryas. But it came more than a century before that cold spell began.

late-132.title: Lake Agassiz, the giant meltwater lake
late-132.text: At its greatest extent, Lake Agassiz may have covered 440,000 km², more than any lake today and about the area of the Black Sea. Fed by meltwater from the retreating Laurentide Ice Sheet, it spread over parts of Manitoba, Ontario, Minnesota, North Dakota and Saskatchewan around 13,000 years ago. From about 13,500 years ago it overflowed south through Glacial River Warren toward the Mississippi. At times it drained east to Lake Superior or northwest to the Arctic. Its huge freshwater releases are thought to have disrupted ocean circulation and affected climate and sea level. One drainage, about 13,000 years ago, has long been the most supported explanation for the {{ref:late-136}}.

late-131.title: The Champlain Sea floods the St. Lawrence
late-131.text: The ice was gone, but the land it had pressed down was still low. About 13,000 years ago rising seas flooded the St. Lawrence and Ottawa valleys, forming the Champlain Sea. About 12,000 years ago, the ice dam holding Lake Vermont failed. The lake dropped 91 m within hours or days before salt water swept in. As the land slowly rebounded, the sea shrank, lasting until about 10,000 years ago.

late-133.title: Hunter-gatherers reach Cyprus
late-133.text: Hunter-gatherers first reached Cyprus around 11,000 to 10,000 BC. The Aetokremnos site may record their hunting of the island's dwarf hippos and dwarf elephants. They also brought wild boar to the island, around 12,000 years ago. Cyprus's dwarf elephant and pygmy hippopotamus later vanished. The genet Genetta plesictoides died out after humans and invasive species arrived.

late-134.title: The Irish elk's brief return
late-134.text: The Irish elk, a giant deer, almost vanished during the Last Glacial Maximum. Few remains date between 27,500 and 14,600 years ago, and none between 23,300 and 17,500. In the warm Bølling–Allerød it recolonized northern Europe. Most Irish remains date to the Allerød, around 13,000 years ago. Then the Younger Dryas cold shrank its range again. By the end of that period, it had vanished from northern Europe.

late-135.title: Pygmy mammoths of the Channel Islands
late-135.text: Columbian mammoths that reached California's Channel Islands shrank into pygmy mammoths, under half the mainland size. They lived there from 80,000 to 13,000 years ago. Their youngest records, about 13,000 years old, coincide with three changes: rising seas shrinking the islands, declining conifer forests and the first people. The people of Arlington Springs Man, on Santa Rosa Island, are thought to have hunted them. Whether climate or hunting mattered more is debated.

late-137.title: The Younger Dryas impact hypothesis
late-137.text: In 2007 Richard Firestone and colleagues proposed a dramatic cause for the {{ref:late-136}}. A comet or meteor impact or airburst about 12,900 years ago, they argued, disrupted Atlantic circulation and also killed off the megafauna. It remains a fringe hypothesis. Most relevant experts reject it for lack of clear evidence. The Hiawatha crater, once linked to it, proved to be 58 million years old.

late-136.title: The Younger Dryas: one last cold snap
late-136.text: In Greenland, the temperature fell by up to 10 °C, and the cooling took three years or less. The Younger Dryas, about 12,900 to 11,700 years ago, was the last cold phase of the Last Glacial Period, a return to glacial conditions. Annual temperatures fell about 3 °C in North America and 2 to 6 °C in Europe. Scientists agree on the mechanism: a severe weakening of the Atlantic overturning circulation, the current that carries heat north. What triggered that weakening is less certain. A meltwater flood from Lake Agassiz and a volcanic trigger are both proposed. The effects rippled worldwide. The Southern Hemisphere warmed, drought hit the region of the African humid period, and lakes on the Altiplano reached a peak. Then it ended as rapidly as it began. Dramatic warming over about 50 years closed the cold spell, and with it the Pleistocene.

late-138.title: Arctodus, the short-faced bear, dies out
late-138.text: Arctodus simus averaged about 625 kg and could reach 957 kg, making it one of the largest land carnivorans ever. It ranged across North America. It vanished from Beringia about 23,000 years ago, during the Last Glacial Maximum, possibly from sharp cooling tied to Heinrich event 2. Elsewhere it lasted until about 12,800 years ago. Plant changes that cut its food supply and competition with brown bears are suggested causes, though the debate continues.

late-139.title: The last scimitar-toothed cats
late-139.text: Homotherium, a lion-sized cat with long, flat, blade-like fangs, weighed up to about 250 kg. For some 4 million years it had lived across North America, Eurasia and Africa. Its youngest well-dated remains, from southern Alberta, are about 12,715 to 12,655 years old. With Smilodon, it was among the last of the saber-toothed machairodonts. Its extinction, like Smilodon's, has been linked to the loss of the big prey it relied on, such as mammoths, bison and horses. Whether climate or hunting drove those losses is debated.

late-140.title: The last Columbian mammoths
late-140.text: Bigger than the woolly mammoth, the Columbian mammoth stood up to 4.2 m tall and weighed up to 12.5 tonnes. It ranged from southern Canada to Costa Rica. Its latest calibrated date, from Colorado's Dent site, is 12,705 to 12,124 years ago, as the Younger Dryas began. No survivors into the Holocene are recorded. Clovis people hunted or scavenged it. Its extinction is blamed on habitat loss from climate change, on human hunting, or on both.

late-141.title: Lake Lahontan at its highest
late-141.text: About 12,700 years ago, Lake Lahontan covered over 22,000 km² of the Great Basin, centered on today's Carson Sink. At this Sehoo highstand it was about 270 m deep near Pyramid Lake. It was one of North America's largest lakes of the last glacial period. Then the changing climate at the end of the Pleistocene began to dry it out.

late-142.title: Castoroides, the giant beaver, dies out
late-142.text: A beaver the size of a bear, weighing about 90 to 125 kg, once lived in North America. Castoroides was the largest known beaver and the continent's largest Pleistocene rodent. It vanished from Alaska and the Yukon after 75,000 years ago. Its last populations lived in the lowlands south of the Great Lakes. The youngest specimens, from New York, date to about 12,050 to 11,501 years ago, overlapping Paleo-Indian artifacts by up to a thousand years.

late-144.title: Pica glass in the Atacama
late-144.text: Patches of natural glass lie in the Atacama Desert, dated to about 12,000 years ago. Where Pica glass came from is unsettled. One account blames a surge in wildfires. A list of possible impact structures counts it as an inferred impact whose crater has not been found.

late-145.title: Macrauchenia, among the last litopterns
late-145.text: Macrauchenia was a long-necked hoofed mammal and one of the last of the Litopterna, an order native to South America for over 60 million years. It died out around 12,000 years ago with most large mammals of the Americas. People had reached South America at least 14,500 years ago. At Paso Otero 5 in the Argentine Pampas, its burned bones lie with Fishtail spear points among other extinct megafauna. Whether hunting or climate change caused its end is debated.

reviews.late-pleistocene-age: The Late Pleistocene began in the warmth of the Eemian, when seas stood 6 to 9 m higher and hippos reached England, and ended with the sudden warming that closed the Younger Dryas. In between, the Last Glacial Period built ice up to 3 km thick, dropped sea level about 125 m and opened land bridges from Beringia to Tasmania. Modern humans used those bridges: one expansion out of Africa about 70,000 to 50,000 years ago carried people to Australia, Europe, Siberia and finally the Americas, mixing with Neanderthals and Denisovans on the way. As they arrived, megafauna vanished, 88% of species in Australia and every mammal over 1,000 kg in the Americas, though how much people and climate each contributed is still debated. When the ice finally melted, meltwater pulses, giant lakes and floods reshaped coasts and rivers.
